name: Grendel
description: The night-stalking monster of the fens who devoured the Danes in their own hall
origin: Anglo-Saxon epic poetry, drawing on Scandinavian legend
legend: Beowulf survives in a single manuscript, written down around the year 1000 and kept for centuries in the library of Sir Robert Cotton, where it was shelved beneath a bust of the emperor Vitellius. In 1731 a fire at Ashburnham House scorched the volume, and its brittle edges have been crumbling ever since, taking words with them. The poem itself is older: scholars still argue whether it was composed in the 700s or nearer the date of the manuscript. Grendel, a descendant of Cain, is maddened by the music and feasting in Heorot, the great hall of Hrothgar, king of the Danes, and raids it by night for twelve years until the Geatish hero Beowulf arrives, refuses to use a sword and tears Grendel's arm off at the shoulder. The poem was first printed in 1815, and J. R. R. Tolkien's 1936 lecture 'Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics' persuaded scholars to read it as a poem rather than a historical scrapbook, monsters and all.

myths.claim: The poem describes Grendel in detail.
myths.explanation: The poet never says what Grendel looks like beyond hints: he is huge, has claws, an ugly light shines from his eyes, and he carries a glove or pouch. Every picture of him is an artist's guess.
The poem says he has laid a spell on weapons so that no blade can bite him, which is why Beowulf fights him bare-handed.
The dragon is a different monster, fought by an aged Beowulf fifty years later. Grendel walks on two legs, like a monstrous man.
The poet says Grendel is of the kin of Cain, the first murderer, from whom sprang the giants, elves and evil spirits that God banished.

myths.claim: Beowulf kills Grendel with a sword.
myths.explanation: He tears off Grendel's arm in a wrestling match, and the monster crawls home to the mere to die. The arm is hung up under Heorot's roof as a trophy.

quotes.text: Grendel this monster grim was called, march-riever mighty, in moorland living, in fen and fastness.
quotes.speaker: Narrator
quotes.source: Beowulf, Francis Gummere's 1910 translation, section I

quotes.text: Then from the moorland, by misty crags, with God's wrath laden, Grendel came.
quotes.speaker: Narrator
quotes.source: Beowulf, Francis Gummere's 1910 translation, section XI

powers: Strength enough to carry off thirty warriors in a night
A spell that blunts every sword
A mother who will avenge him
weaknesses: Bare hands and a very firm grip
Music, feasting and joy, which he cannot bear
legacy: Grendel (1971), John Gardner's novel that tells the story from the monster's side
Seamus Heaney's translation (1999), which won the Whitbread Book of the Year
Beowulf & Grendel (2005), filmed in Iceland with Gerard Butler
Beowulf (2007), Robert Zemeckis's motion-capture film with Crispin Glover as Grendel
facts: Beowulf survives in a single manuscript, scorched in the Ashburnham House fire of 1731
Grendel attacks Heorot, the mead hall of Hrothgar, king of the Danes
He raids the hall for twelve years before Beowulf arrives
On his first raid he carries off thirty warriors
Beowulf fights him bare-handed and tears off his arm
The poem calls Grendel a descendant of Cain
The poem runs to 3,182 lines and was first printed in 1815
hostIntro: Tonight's guest doesn't care for singing, feasting or lights left on after dark, so keep the applause brief. He's come a long way from the fens, and he's hungry.
